cards.front: How wide is the latency gap between the fastest and slowest tiers in a data center?
cards.back: L1 cache is ~1 ns and a cross-continent round trip is ~100 ms — a 100,000,000x (10^8) end-to-end gap across seven tiers (L1, RAM, SSD, in-DC network, disk, cross-region, cross-continent).

cards.front: In what sense is a query plan a "routing decision"?
cards.back: It decides which latency tier data is read from, how often, and in what order. Get the tier right and a billion-row query finishes in seconds; get it wrong and it never finishes.

cards.front: What is a page, and what are the typical page sizes?
cards.back: The fixed-size unit of transfer between SSD/disk and RAM. Classic Unix and relational DBs like PostgreSQL use 8 KB pages; big-data systems use 64 MB.

cards.front: Why do big-data algorithms count pages instead of bytes?
cards.back: One IO moves one full page and costs the same whether you need one byte or the whole 64 MB. Since cost is per page moved, minimizing page count is what matters.

cards.front: If an L1 cache hit were rescaled to 1 second, how long would RAM, SSD, and HDD reads take?
cards.back: RAM ≈ 1.5 minutes, SSD ≈ 3 hours, HDD ≈ 4 months. Paging fights this gap by keeping the working set in RAM.

cards.front: What two numbers define IO cost, and what are the throughput values for RAM/SSD/HDD?
cards.back: Access latency (fixed startup overhead per IO, independent of size) and throughput (sustained transfer rate): RAM ~100 GB/s, SSD ~5 GB/s, HDD ~100 MB/s.

cards.front: Why can't a faster GPU fix a slow scan over a 1 TB dataset?
cards.back: Compute is effectively free (~312 TFLOPS ⇒ ~0 time), but the links feeding it are narrow: PCIe ~32 GB/s, SSD ~5 GB/s. Reading 1 TB across PCIe takes ~30 s; servers add capacity, never link speed.

cards.front: What is the IO cost model formula for an algorithm's runtime?
cards.back: Cost = C_r × pages_read + C_w × pages_written. On data larger than RAM, IO dominates and everything else (CPU work) rounds to zero.

cards.front: Small data vs big data: what is the bottleneck in each regime?
cards.back: Small data (under ~1 GB, fits in RAM): CPU complexity, e.g. O(n log n). Big data (over ~100 GB): IO complexity — moving data costs ~a million times more than CPU ops, so you minimize disk touches.

cards.front: In IO cost notation, what do T(R) and P(R) mean, and roughly how much CPU work does saving one IO buy?
cards.back: T(R) = number of tuples (rows) in table R; P(R) = number of pages. Saving one IO saves about 10 million CPU/GPU operations.

cards.front: What is the formula for the cost of reading one page, C_r?
cards.back: C_r = Access Time + (Page Size ÷ Scan Speed). Total read cost = numPages × C_r (writes use C_w the same way).

cards.front: What are the course's C_r values for one 64 MB page on RAM, SSD, and HDD?
cards.back: RAM 0.00064 s, SSD 0.01281 s, HDD 0.65 s (network 0.00641 s). For 64 MB pages the transfer term dominates the access term.

cards.front: MB vs MiB — which does CS145 use for calculations?
cards.back: MB/GB are decimal (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes); MiB/GiB are binary (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes). All CS145 problems use decimal MB/GB consistently.

cards.front: With a 90% RAM hit rate, why can total read time still be dominated by disk?
cards.back: The slowest tier dominates whenever anything falls through to it: in the course example, 5 HDD pages out of 200 (2.5% of requests) take 3.25 s of the 3.57 s total — 91% of the time.

cards.front: How does reading a page from another machine's RAM compare to reading from local SSD?
cards.back: Network RAM ≈ 0.0077 s (remote read + network transfer + local write) beats local SSD ≈ 0.0128 s. That's why distributed in-memory caches (Memcached, Redis Cluster) beat SSD-backed databases for hot reads.

cards.front: How many 64 MB pages does the Spotify Songs table (500M rows × 1024 bytes) occupy?
Define hashing and its three key properties.
cards.back: Hashing maps an input of any size to a fixed-size value in [0, B-1]. It is deterministic (same input → same output), aims for uniform spread (expected O(1) access), and is one-way — it is not compression.

cards.front: What are the two standard fixes for hash collisions, and what load factor keeps them cheap?
cards.back: Chaining (a linked list at each bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next empty slot). Keep the load factor n/B under about 0.75 to bound lookup cost.

cards.front: By the birthday paradox, after how many inserts does a B-bucket hash table hit a 50% collision chance?
cards.back: About √B inserts — just as 23 people make a shared birthday likely. Collisions are unavoidable long before the table looks full.

cards.front: Why is summing ASCII codes a bad string hash, and what does production code use instead?
cards.back: Any reordering of the same characters sums identically, so anagrams collide. The polynomial rolling hash weights each character by a power of a prime (P = 31), making order matter and spreading keys evenly.

cards.front: What does geo-hashing do to a (lat, lng) coordinate?
cards.back: It converts the 2-D coordinate into a 1-D grid-cell key, so nearby points share a code and "find within 2 km" becomes a few cell lookups instead of distance math over millions of rows. It is an exact spatial hash.

cards.front: Why hexagons instead of squares for geo-hash grids (Uber H3)?
cards.back: A hexagon's six neighbours are all exactly the same distance from the centre, so the ring a radius query reads is even in every direction. A square's four corner-neighbours sit √2 farther than its edge-neighbours, making the ring lopsided.

cards.front: What does a geo-hashed radius query cost, and why is that the win?
cards.back: Up to seven cell lookups — the query's cell plus its six neighbours (the radius crosses borders) — possibly on seven different pages. The win is that seven is constant whether there are ten thousand orders or ten million.

cards.front: Run-length encoding (RLE): what does it store and when does it shine?
cards.back: It collapses a run of repeated values into (value, count), e.g. Mickey × 100M. Ratios of 10x–100x are normal on columns physically sorted so the same value lingers; the runs come from the sort order on disk.

cards.front: Dictionary encoding: what does it store and when does it shine?
cards.back: Replace each value with a small integer index into a dictionary. Best for low-cardinality columns: a genre column with ~50 distinct values stores a 1-byte code instead of a 16-byte string — a 16x win.

cards.front: Delta encoding: what does it store and when does it shine?
cards.back: For sorted numeric columns, store differences between consecutive values instead of the values. Timestamps microseconds apart become tiny deltas that fit in 1-byte ints instead of 8-byte longs; auto-increment IDs and sensor readings benefit too.

cards.front: How do compression techniques compound, and what condition makes it work?
cards.back: Run them in sequence, each on the previous output: RLE (4 MB → 200 KB), then dictionary (→ 100 KB), then zstd entropy-coding the leftover byte patterns (→ 50 KB), a 98.75% reduction. It requires the column to be physically sorted/clustered and low-cardinality — otherwise almost none of it happens.

cards.front: What two answers can a Bloom filter give, and which error type is impossible?
cards.back: "Definitely not in the set" (any hashed bit is 0) or "probably in the set" (all bits 1). False positives are possible; false negatives never are — inserting an item would have set all its bits.

cards.front: What is the Bloom filter sizing rule of thumb?
cards.back: 10 bits per item with optimal k ≈ 7 hash functions gives about a 1% false-positive rate — the sweet spot. (4 bits ⇒ ~15%, 14 bits ⇒ ~0.1%.)

cards.front: How does a Bloom filter save IOs in a database?
cards.back: Before reading a page, ask the filter "is the key here?" A "no" is guaranteed, so you skip the read; a "maybe" triggers the real read. Almost every true miss avoids its page read, at ~10 bits per item instead of a full hash set.

cards.front: How much smaller is Chrome's Safe Browsing Bloom filter than the raw blocklist?
cards.back: 100M URLs × 80 bytes ≈ 8 GB raw; the Bloom filter at 10 bits/item is 125 MB — about 64x smaller, with ~1% false positives — small enough to ship to 3 billion devices.

cards.front: What is the k-anonymity trick in Chrome Safe Browsing?
cards.back: On a "maybe," Chrome sends only a 32-bit prefix of the URL's hash; Google returns all malicious hashes sharing that prefix and Chrome finishes the match locally. Safe URLs are answered locally with nothing sent, so Google never sees your URL.

cards.front: How does locality-sensitive hashing differ from an ordinary hash?
cards.back: An ordinary hash scatters similar inputs apart on purpose; LSH sends similar vectors to the same bucket, so "find things like this" reads one bucket instead of scanning everything. Closeness survives the hash.

cards.front: How does LSH turn random hyperplanes into a bucket code, and what does it cost?
cards.back: Each random cut asks one yes/no question — which side is the point on — contributing one bit. Near points agree on almost every cut, so they share a k-bit code and bucket. Search drops from O(N) to about O(N / 2^k), at the price of occasionally missing a close pair that straddles a cut.

cards.front: What does the number of hyperplanes k trade off in LSH, and how do systems recover lost pairs?
cards.back: More hyperplanes make purer buckets but split more true pairs — k trades recall for selectivity. Systems union several independent hash tables to recover the pairs any single table drops.

cards.front: LSH vs quantization: which problem does each shrink?
cards.back: LSH shrinks the search (look in one bucket instead of all N). Quantization shrinks the storage: replace each exact value with a small bucket code so a kilobytes-size vector takes a handful of bytes, keeping just enough to preserve who is near whom.

cards.front: What is approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search, and why do vector databases use it?
cards.back: ANN gives up the guarantee of the exact closest vectors for an answer that's almost always right and far cheaper. Exact search is O(N) per query (~1.5B multiply-adds, ~6 GB scanned per million 1,536-D vectors); an ANN index looks at only the vectors near the query, in sub-millisecond time.

cards.front: IVF vs HNSW: how does each ANN index skip the full scan?
cards.back: IVF k-means the vectors into cells and probes only the few nearest cells. HNSW builds a hierarchy of proximity graphs — long-range links on top, short local links at layer 0 — and a query greedy-hops down toward itself. Both are built once at index time; HNSW is the common production default (best recall per millisecond, more memory).

cards.front: What is TurboQuant's recipe for compressing a billion embeddings?
cards.back: Spin, then round: apply one random rotation to spread the information evenly across coordinates (moving no point, changing no distance), then round each coordinate to a few bits. Shrinks the index 8–32x with little loss, on any data, with no codebook to train.

cards.front: What are the two levers for a problem too big to scan or store, and their exact/approximate variants?
cards.back: Lever 1, don't scan all N: partition the lookup — exact = hash to one bucket; approximate = prune what's definitely absent (Bloom) or bucket by similarity (LSH, IVF, HNSW). Lever 2, don't store all N bytes: shrink each item — lossless = drop redundancy (RLE, dictionary, delta, bit packing); lossy = drop precision but keep rank order (PQ, TurboQuant). Production composes both: IVF-PQ is the vector database.
